content.text:
The question has two levels. First, is there unseen matter at all, or does gravity need changing? Second, if the matter exists, what is it? I treat the first as a separate baseline and rank the specific candidates below it. All dates are as of November 2026.

## 0. Baseline: cold dark matter of unknown identity (the standard ΛCDM cosmological model)

**Status.** The Atacama Cosmology Telescope collaboration (Louis et al., "DR6 Power Spectra, Likelihoods and ΛCDM Parameters", *JCAP*, 2025) found excellent agreement with ΛCDM. Their result is independent of Planck. Combined with the DESI DR2 galaxy-survey data, the two agree at 1.6σ. Euclid published its first dark-matter map of a galaxy cluster in 2026 (Schrabback et al., *A&A*, 2026); its first cosmology results are due in 2027.

There is a live tension on small scales. Natarajan, Chiang & Dutra ("New Cold Dark Matter Crisis Revealed by Multiscale Cluster Lensing", *ApJ Letters*, 2026) find that the overall count of clumps inside clusters by mass matches CDM. However, real clusters contain more clumps near their centres than simulated CDM clusters do.

**Verdict: solid**
**Principal problem:** none (it doesn't say what dark matter is)
Strongest: many unrelated probes (the cosmic microwave background (CMB), galaxy clustering, lensing, clusters) agree quantitatively, across many countries and instruments.
Weakest: tensions on galaxy and cluster scales, and the particle itself is unknown.
Worth checking further: Euclid's 2027 results, and whether the cluster-substructure tension survives better treatment of ordinary-matter physics in simulations.
Best objection to this verdict: the AeST theory (below) shows a modified-gravity model can also fit the CMB, so the evidence is less one-sided than it looks.

## 1. WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles)

**Status.** No direct detection yet:
- **LZ:** found no WIMPs in 417 live days of data (March 2023 to April 2025; LZ Collaboration, December 2025). It also began detecting solar neutrinos, which form a background ("neutrino fog") that will increasingly mask WIMP signals.
- **XENONnT:** no signal in 3.1 tonne-years ("WIMP Dark Matter Search Using a 3.1 Tonne-Year Exposure", *PRL*, 2025).
- **PandaX-4T:** no signal in 1.54 tonne-years (*PRL*, 2025).
- **DAMA's long-claimed signal:** two experiments using the same crystal, COSINE-100 (*Science Advances*, 2025) and ANAIS-112 (6 years of data, 2025), see no annual modulation.

Two new hints have appeared:
- **Gamma rays from the Milky Way halo.** Totani ("20 GeV halo-like excess…", *JCAP*, 2025) reported an excess, as a single author. Stenhouse, Ghag & Deppisch reproduced it independently (arXiv:2607.08552, 2026). Abazajian, Li & Macias (arXiv:2610.23713, 2026) find that its significance swings from about 1σ to 18σ depending on how the background emission is modelled. Cosmic-ray antiproton data from the AMS-02 detector also constrain it (arXiv:2512.12176).
- **One LZ event.** A single nuclear recoil at about 248 keV, at 3.4σ local and 2.6σ global significance (LZ, arXiv:2609.02823, 2026). Linking it to the gamma-ray excess (a roughly 420 GeV particle) is an after-the-fact fit.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** headline predictions failed; survives by retreating to smaller interaction strengths
Strongest: the largest, most international and best-equipped programme. Rival xenon experiments in the US/UK, Europe/Japan and China can check each other, and DarkSide-20k is under construction.
Weakest: the original expectation of particles interacting at weak-force strength has not been met. From my own background knowledge (not checked here), the LHC has also found no supersymmetric partners. Both hints are weak.
Worth checking further: whether XENONnT and PandaX see anything in the same high-energy recoil window, and gamma-ray limits from dwarf galaxies.
Best objection to this verdict: two partly independent hints point at a similar mass. That arguably makes this "inconclusive (balance)" rather than fragile.

## 2. QCD axion

**Status.**
- ADMX reached the sensitivity needed for benchmark axion models over 1.10–1.31 GHz (*PRL*, 2025).
- HAYSTAC Phase II ran the widest search yet using quantum "squeezing" to beat noise (*PRL* 134, 151006, 2025).
- Further groups work in Korea (CAPP) and Europe (MADMAX, QUAX, RADES).
- The motivation is independent of dark matter: the axion would also solve the strong-CP problem in particle physics.

**Verdict: defensible**
**Principal problem:** none
Strongest: independently motivated, with interaction strengths predicted in advance and tested without being moved.
Weakest: the mass is not predicted, and only thin slices of the plausible range have been scanned, so a null result refutes little.
Worth checking further: whether theoretical mass predictions converge, and the higher-frequency experiments.
Best objection to this verdict: it is "unrefuted" partly because it is hard to test.

## 3. Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM)

**Status.**
- The idea is that dark-matter particles scatter off each other, smoothing halo centres into cores.
- Cluster collisions limit how strongly they can interact, so models make the interaction depend on velocity (Particle Data Group, "Dark Matter" review, 2025).
- Evidence is equivocal. Diego's *A&A* 2026 study of the cluster AS1063 is titled "possible evidence… or not". Cores in ultra-faint dwarf galaxies are now being used to constrain the models (*A&A*, 2025).

**Verdict: inconclusive (evidence)**
**Principal problem:** its signatures are hard to tell apart from ordinary-matter effects such as supernova feedback
Strongest: it addresses real small-scale data.
Weakest: velocity dependence plus "core collapse" can fit almost any pattern of halo shapes, which is adjustment after the fact.
Worth checking further: SIDM simulations tested against the Natarajan cluster-lensing results.
Best objection to this verdict: it is an extension of CDM, not a rival to it.

## 4. Ultralight ("fuzzy") dark matter

**Status.** Lyman-α forest data (absorption in distant quasar light, which traces small-scale structure) require a particle mass above 1.9×10⁻²¹ eV (*JCAP*, September 2026). That disfavours the original 10⁻²² eV version, which was chosen to solve small-scale problems. Heavier versions remain viable.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** the mass that motivated it is excluded
Strongest: clean theory with distinctive wave-like predictions.
Weakest: the version that survives looks almost like CDM on the scales we can observe.
Worth checking further: how the bound depends on modelling the gas between galaxies.
Best objection to this verdict: those modelling uncertainties are real.

## 5. Primordial black holes (PBHs)

**Status.**
- Gravitational microlensing rules out compact objects over a wide mass range (Mróz et al., 20 years of OGLE data, *ApJS*, 2025).
- Only the "asteroid-mass window" (about 10¹⁷–10²³ g) remains open (Springer chapter "The Asteroid Mass Window", 2025).
- LIGO–Virgo–KAGRA's candidate merger S251112cm involves an object lighter than the Sun, which stars cannot make. But its false-alarm rate is about 0.16 per year, and one analysis thinks a real astrophysical source is unlikely (arXiv:2607.24951).

**Verdict: inconclusive (evidence)**
**Principal problem:** viable only where we can't yet test it; needs unusual early-universe physics
Strongest: needs no new particle; gravitational-wave detectors give a genuine discovery channel.
Weakest: no positive evidence that PBHs make up all the dark matter.
Worth checking further: the final O4 search for lighter-than-Sun objects.
Best objection to this verdict: it has no outright failed prediction, unlike the programmes ranked above it.

## 6. keV sterile neutrinos (warm dark matter)

**Status.** XRISM stacked 3.75 Ms of observations of ten galaxy clusters and found no unexplained lines (XRISM Collaboration, arXiv:2510.24560, 2025). Its limit is 3–4 times tighter than Hitomi's, but still about 5 times above the 3.5 keV line Bulbul et al. claimed in 2014. Lyman-α and satellite-galaxy counts also squeeze warm dark matter.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** its one positive signal (the 3.5 keV line) has not been confirmed
Strongest: sterile neutrinos are a natural explanation for neutrino masses.
Weakest: production mechanisms have been tuned to fit both the line and the structure bounds.
Worth checking further: XRISM data stacked over several years.
Best objection to this verdict: XRISM is not yet decisive.

## 7. MOND and relativistic versions (no dark matter)

**Status.**
- **Galaxies:** a strong record of predictions made in advance. Weak lensing shows rotation curves staying flat out to about 1 Mpc (Mistele, Lelli & McGaugh, 2024).
- **Wide binary stars, the decisive local test:** Chae et al. (2026) reported gravity about 1.6 times Newtonian, using 36 binaries. Saad & Ting's reanalysis of the same sample gives γ = 1.00 (+0.24 −0.19), i.e. Newtonian (*Open Journal of Astrophysics*, 2026). An independent 65-system study also finds no anomaly (arXiv:2610.28220). Banik et al. (*MNRAS*, 2024) strongly favoured Newton; Hernandez & Kroupa (*MNRAS*, 2025) dispute this.
- **Clusters:** MOND still needs unseen mass in cluster cores. Combes (arXiv:2611.08702, November 2026) proposes dark baryons; Zhang, Hasani Zonoozi & Kroupa (*PRD*, 2026) propose stellar remnants.
- **Cosmology:** AeST (Skordis & Złośnik, 2021) fits the CMB, but only by adding a field that behaves like dark matter.
- **Community:** a few groups.

**Verdict: fragile**
**Principal problem:** still needs unseen mass in clusters and cosmology
Strongest: the best record of advance predictions at galaxy scale of any programme here.
Weakest: cluster and CMB fixes are added after the fact, and wide binaries are trending Newtonian.
Worth checking further: Gaia DR4 (expected around the end of 2026), and direct searches for cluster dark baryons.
Best objection to this verdict: CDM's own galaxy-scale fits also rely on tuned feedback, so MOND is held to a stricter standard.

## Ranking (specific programmes, best to worst)

| Rank | Programme | Evidence | Fits rest of physics | Active | Breadth | Prediction record |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Axion | none yet, little excluded | strong | yes | moderate, international | predicted, untested |
| 2 | WIMP | weak hints, many nulls | strong | very | widest | key predictions failed |
| 3 | SIDM | ambiguous | good | yes | moderate | flexible |
| 4 | Fuzzy | bounded | good | yes | moderate | core version excluded |
| 5 | PBH | none (window open) | needs special early universe | yes | broad | none tested |
| 6 | Sterile ν | signal unconfirmed | good | modest | moderate | fading |
| 7 | MOND | strong in galaxies, poor in clusters/CMB | poor without extras | yes | concentrated | best at galaxies, fails elsewhere |

- **Axion above WIMP:** similar breadth and coherence, but the axion's predictions are untested where the WIMP's have failed.
- **WIMP above SIDM:** much stronger instruments, and it can actually be falsified.
- **SIDM above the rest:** it is the only one with a free parameter that still explains something.
- **Fuzzy, PBH, sterile neutrinos:** each has lost its original motivation or signal, or is confined to an untested window.
- **MOND last:** as a full replacement for dark matter, it conflicts with the strongest evidence. That is despite having the best galaxy-scale record of all.

**Best objection to this ranking:** it favours programmes that have made fewer risky predictions. MOND and WIMPs stuck their necks out, and the axion has barely been tested. Applied the other way, ranking by successful predictions made in advance would put MOND near the top.

**Where I'm unsure:**
- The axion/WIMP order. Confirmation of the LZ event or the halo excess would flip it.
- The order of places 4–6.
- Putting SIDM in the same ranking at all, since it extends CDM rather than competing with it.
